title: Christmas at Maxwell's
full_review:
Here's the latest entry in that most popular of cinematic genres: the Christmas movie.

"Christmas at Maxwell's" (LauferFilm) concerns wine merchant Andrew Austin (Andrew May), who is coping with the cancer-related illness of his wife, Suzie (Jack Hourigan), while trying to raise their two children, Chris and Mary (Charlie and Julia May). With the holidays approaching, Andrew can't understand why he doesn't "feel anything anymore." (Of course, a gravely ill wife might have something to do with it.)

He starts drinking, but manages to resist the temptations of a former flame (Lauren Dowden) to "relieve his frustration" and go home with her.

There are several flashbacks that outline his courtship of Suzie: They knew each other in college, grew apart, she became a singer in New York (several musical sequences with a now-robust Hourigan demonstrating her vocal chops), and though they both had romantic involvements they came together again. But there was a catch: She was pregnant with another man's child. Therein lies part of the secret that so torments Andrew. Still, until Suzie was stricken with cancer, they had a good life, with Suzie giving singing lessons as an outlet for her talent, and sometimes magnanimously refusing payment.

Profoundly unhappy and struggling with heavy guilt about that mysterious past event, Andrew takes the family to their summer home -- Maxwell's Hospitality House (thus, the title) -- on Lake Erie in a desperate attempt to rekindle the Christmas spirit.

Matters are at their bleakest -- as is the medical prognosis -- when a lovable old nursing home resident (Angus May), whom they (improbably) take in for the holidays, effects a miraculous change in their lives.

Inspired by personal experience, director-writer William C. Laufer (who also plays a priest to whom Andrew goes for counseling) has made a heartfelt film -- clearly, a labor of love -- with admirable messages about God's forgiveness, the strength of family and being a good Samaritan, with a touching conclusion. But the film is handicapped by languid pacing, an episodic script and mostly colorless performances -- except perhaps for Hourigan, who conveys some variety.

The picturesque film was shot in various Cleveland locales.

The film contains mild profanity, crass expressions and mature thematic material. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
